scores.fix: Real people barely play AI songs, but bots do.
scores.note: Hits three Never-say rows (AI songs as the thief, every AI song takes money, 'nobody listens' as the problem) and breaks the one-sentence, 12-word rule.

scores.fix: Some days, over half the new songs on one app are AI-made.
scores.note: The cover drops 'one app' and 'some days', so it reads as half of all new music, and song counts aren't the mechanism (the pot splits plays).

scores.fix: Keep the line; cover: BOTS PLAYED HIS AI SONGS. 18 MONTHS.
scores.note: One real person, a real sentence and the itch 'who did he even hurt?' that leads straight to the pot; the truest strong hook here, held back only by a clunky cover that drops 'AI'.

scores.fix: An AI song can get paid without a single real listener.
scores.note: A true paradox that leads cleanly to bots and the pot, but with no AI, no person and no 'you' it misses the fuss.

scores.fix: Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's pay.
scores.note: Plain, personal and true with the payoff on frame 0, but 'can' and 'paycheck' soften the cover and AI is missing.

scores.fix: Some of your subscription can go to songs only bots play.
scores.note: True and personal, but the surprise is the pro-rata model rather than fake plays, so the bot turn arrives late.
A near-duplicate of L35 whose singular line doesn't match its plural cover.

scores.fix: Why would anyone upload AI songs just for bots to play?
scores.note: A good puzzle, but it states one app's view as fact, says 'make' where the evidence says 'upload', and without 'AI' the cover is cryptic.
True with its scope, but a report headline with no person, no 'you' and no picture.
A heist picture with a real number, but 'want' is limp and a single $11 billion pile hints at one global pot.

scores.fix: The biggest fans of AI songs? On one app, bots.
scores.note: The best cover of the 'fans' pair and honestly scoped, but opening the voice on 'On one app' wastes the first second.
It names the mechanism, but 'the pot' means nothing at a glance, the present tense claims more than we can show, and the cover drops the 'you'.
A big number plus a twist, but 'mostly for bots' is one app's view stated as fact, and the cover drops 'nearly' and 'one app'.

scores.fix: The plays are fake, but the money they skim is real. (cover: FAKE PLAYS. REAL MONEY.)
scores.note: The best-designed three-beat cover in the set, but chaining AI songs to fake plays edges toward 'AI songs are fraud', and the spoken line is writerly.
Clever over plain: two sentences and a wordplay leap from your ears to the app's filters.

scores.fix: Some of your fee can end up with bots.
scores.note: The right idea with true hedges, but 12 words of 'some ... can end up paying for' bury the sting.

scores.fix: Who pays when bots play AI songs on repeat?
scores.note: More concrete than L35 but longer, and the tacked-on 'so who pays?' reads less naturally.
The best ride on the fuss and the most comment bait, but the pot doesn't answer 'could you tell?' and we can't play a test, so the turn risks a bait-and-switch.

scores.fix: Part of your subscription can pay a bot farm.
scores.note: 'Bot farm' is the most vivid noun in the money family and its cover is the truest, but the spoken line is wordy.
A smart loophole, but it explains the trick before the viewer has a reason to care.

scores.fix: One app says most AI uploads are for bots, not you.
scores.note: It stretches one app's 'main purpose for uploading' into 'most AI songs aren't made for you', and the cover drops the attribution.
The most accurate statement of the payoff, but the qualifier eats the punch and 'UNCAUGHT' makes a heavy cover.
Plain, true and personal, but it hooks on the pro-rata model with no AI and no bots on frame 0.
The cleanest, most natural 'you' line here, but it promises a reveal about your taste and the video is about fake plays.
A good triad cover, but 'your apps' is a stake nobody feels and the line stacks three owners (one man's, his, your).

scores.fix: Keep the line; cover: THE BIGGEST AI SONG FANS? BOTS. with a small 'one app, 2025' credit, and 'on one app' in line 2.
scores.note: The most shareable picture in the set and it begs 'why would bots be fans?', but as written it generalizes one app's 2025 numbers.

scores.fix: Keep it; put a small 'prosecutors say' on the cover and land 'his own bots did the playing' by ~2 s.
scores.note: The sharpest whiplash and the best Smith cover, but 'billions' is the prosecutors' figure and all bot plays, so it reads like a jailed hitmaker until the reveal.

scores.fix: An AI song nobody hears can still get paid.
scores.note: A clean, true paradox that rides AI and points at 'whose money?', with a softer sting than the top lines.
A wink without a sting, and 'all these AI songs' implies plays they mostly don't get.

scores.fix: Real people barely play AI songs, so who does?
scores.note: An honest puzzle, but a slow conditional with no stake, and its cover answers the question the voice asks.
A chart, not a hook: two numbers and no subject on the cover, pointing at 'nobody listens', which isn't the problem.
The safe wording, but attribution first and a dull verb make it a report, not a hook.
Accurate, but 'on one app, up to' hedges the big number's punch away, and the cover needs the year.
The plainest bold claim, with the payoff on frame 0 and 'skimming' sizing it honestly; it asserts that fakes slip through now (FL 8.2 allows that), and AI has to arrive in line 2.
Short, true, and the whole video is its answer, but a riddle needs the frame-0 picture to bring the jolt.

scores.fix: Keep the line; cover: PART OF YOUR FEE CAN PAY BOTS (keeps the 'some').
scores.note: The tightest 'your money' line, but 'some ... can' hedges the voice, the cover drops 'some', and free-tier viewers have no subscription.

scores.fix: What a fake play earns comes out of real artists' pay.
scores.note: The payoff itself as an aphorism: neat and self-qualifying, but abstract, and the ellipsis slows the read.

scores.fix: Cover: BOTS PLAYED HIS AI SONGS. WHO LOST OUT?
scores.note: It turns the contested harm into an honest question, but 'one man's' is vague and 'BOT-PLAYED' is an awkward cover.
An eerie idea that's too abstract at a glance: 'plays you never hear' needs explaining.
One real person in his own words, but an executive and a finance term: right for a mid-video quote card, not for frame 0.
Concrete numbers in his own words, but with no AI, no victim and no consequence the cover reads like a get-rich tip.
L3 without the AI songs and with a vaguer verb.
Attributed, but it puts the contested 'robbed' on frame 0 without the defence, and 'and their fans' is hard to pay off in 40 s.
A gripping real story about a different problem, impersonation, which the pot can't pay off.
A great mid-video quote card (his own 'TON'), but as frame 0 it's a con with no victim and no one for 'his' to point to.
Uncanny but context-free, and impersonation is the strand the pot can't pay off.
Hayduk's logic in jargon ('pads', 'slop'), and it blames AI slop instead of fake plays.
